lesson.intro: Halftime. The new has worn off, the routines are real, and the progress report is your scoreboard at the half. Here's what the four words look like in the second half.

cards.heading: Read it, don't fear it
cards.body: A progress report is halftime, not the final. Read it for one thing to fix, then fix that one thing.

cards.heading: Habits beat moods
cards.body: Some nights you won't feel like it. Start anyway, at the time you always do. Starting is the hard part.

cards.heading: Argue with the idea
cards.body: Disagree all you want. Give a reason, and leave the person out of it.

cards.heading: Same work, any adult
cards.body: Sub today? The plan is still the plan. The work counts, and so does the adult running the room.

cards.heading: Stop it with you
cards.body: You can't unsend a screenshot, but you can be the one who doesn't pass it on.

cards.heading: Ten seconds
cards.body: The groups have settled. If someone's still on their own, say hi. It takes ten seconds.

cards.heading: Phone across the room
cards.body: The nights are longer now. Put the phone across the room at bedtime. A rested brain remembers more.

cards.heading: Stay out of the pile-on
cards.body: When the comments turn mean, don't add fuel. Check on the person privately, and tell an adult if it keeps going.

cards.heading: More than a bad day
cards.body: Everyone has bad days. If it's been a couple of weeks, tell an adult you trust. Saying so early is how things start to get better.

practice.intro: Twelve situations for the second half. Pick the choice that fits the four words best.

items.question: Progress reports come out. One skill is lower than you wanted. What's the best first step?

choices.text: Decide history just isn't your thing.
Wait for the next marking period to start fresh.
Redo everything at once this weekend.
Pick that one skill and ask what would raise it one step.

hints: Which one is small enough to actually do this week?
Which one uses what the progress report told you?
items.reasoning: One change you'll actually make beats ten you won't. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.A: A skill shows where you are now, not who you are.
distractors.B: The work you do now still counts. Waiting skips chances you already have.
distractors.C: Ten changes by Sunday usually means none by Wednesday.

items.question: It's a school night, and you don't feel like doing the reading. What works best?

choices.text: Skip it. You'll do better when you feel like it.
Start at your usual time, even if it's just the first page.
Save it all for the night before the test.
Ask a friend what it said instead.

hints: Which choice doesn't depend on your mood?
What gets easier once you've started?
items.reasoning: Habits carry you on the days motivation doesn't show up. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.A: The feeling might never show up. The reading still will.
distractors.C: One night can't hold a whole unit.
distractors.D: Their summary is their thinking, not yours.

items.question: You've been lost in class for a week, and the test is next week. When do you ask for help?

choices.text: Now, while there's still time to fix it.
The day before the test.
After the test, once you see how it went.
Never. Asking makes it look like you weren't paying attention.

hints: When does help have the most time to work?
Which choice gets you unstuck before it counts?
items.reasoning: Asking early gives help time to work. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.B: One day isn't enough to catch up on a week.
distractors.C: After the test, the help comes too late for that test.
distractors.D: Asking means you noticed what you don't get. That is paying attention.

items.question: In a class discussion, you think someone's point is flat wrong. What's the best way in?

choices.text: "That makes no sense."
Roll your eyes and wait for the teacher to fix it.
"I see it differently. Here's why."
Say nothing, then complain about it after class.

hints: Which choice argues with the idea, not the person?
Which one gives a reason?
items.reasoning: Disagree with the idea, give a reason, and leave the person out of it. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.A: It gives no reason, and it lands on the person.
distractors.B: An eye roll says plenty, and none of it helps.
distractors.D: The class never hears your side, and the complaint helps nobody.

items.question: You get paired with someone you don't really get along with. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask to switch before you even start.
Keep it about the work, and do it together.
Split it up so you never have to talk.
Let them do it all. It's their problem.

hints: Which choice still gets the work done well?
What will you have to do at a job someday?
items.reasoning: You don't have to be friends to work well together. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.A: Give it a real try first. If it still isn't working, a teacher will step in.
distractors.C: Two halves that never met don't make one good answer.
distractors.D: Then your name is on work you didn't do.

items.question: There's a substitute today. The plan says to do the reading and answer the questions. What do you do?

choices.text: Do the work like it's any other day.
Treat it like a free period. The sub won't know.
Tell the sub your teacher never makes you do this.
Do half, and save the rest for when your teacher's back.

hints: Which choice would look the same if your teacher walked in?
Whose plan is the sub following?
items.reasoning: The work and the adult running the room get the same respect every day. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.B: The work still counts, and so does the adult in the room.
distractors.C: Making up rules puts the sub in a bad spot and you in a worse one.
distractors.D: Tomorrow comes with its own work.

items.question: A rumor about someone is going around the group chat. You don't know if it's true. What do you do?

choices.text: Pass it on, but add "idk if this is true."
Ask the chat who started it.
Don't pass it on, and don't add to it.
Screenshot it in case it turns out to be true.

hints: Which choice stops it with you?
What would you want if the rumor were about you?
items.reasoning: A rumor stops when someone stops passing it. Be that someone. That's Be Kind.

distractors.A: "idk" doesn't unsend it. It still spreads.
distractors.B: Chasing who started it keeps everyone talking about it.
distractors.D: A screenshot is one more copy.

items.question: The lunch groups have settled. Someone has been sitting alone for weeks. What could you do?

choices.text: Nothing. They probably like it that way.
Wait for someone else to do something.
Talk about it with your friends, and leave it there.
Say hi, or ask if they want to sit with you.

hints: Which choice takes ten seconds and costs you nothing?
What would it feel like to be the one sitting alone?
items.reasoning: A hello takes ten seconds and can change someone's whole week. That's Be Kind.

distractors.A: Maybe. Asking is the only way to find out.
distractors.B: If everyone waits for someone else, nobody goes.
distractors.C: Talking about someone isn't the same as talking to them.

items.question: You get a paper back, and it didn't go well. What's the most helpful thing to tell yourself?

choices.text: "I'm just bad at this."
"It doesn't matter anyway."
"That one didn't go well. What's one thing I can fix next time?"
"I'm never looking at that again."

hints: Which one would you say to a friend?
Which one gives you something to do next?
items.reasoning: Talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a friend: honest, then helpful. That's Be Kind.

distractors.A: That's where you are today, not where you have to stay.
distractors.B: It does matter. That's why it stings, and why it's worth fixing.
distractors.D: The notes on it are the map to the next one.

items.question: It's 1 a.m., you're still scrolling, and you have a test tomorrow. What's the best call?

choices.text: Phone across the room, lights out.
Stay up and study, since you're awake anyway.
One more video, then sleep.
Keep scrolling. You'll catch up on sleep this weekend.

hints: Which choice gets you the most sleep from here?
Which one takes the phone out of reach?
items.reasoning: A rested brain remembers more. Sleep is part of getting ready. That's Be Safe.

distractors.B: Studying at 1 a.m. trades the sleep you need for notes you won't remember.
distractors.C: "One more" is how it got to be 1 a.m.
distractors.D: The weekend doesn't help tomorrow's test.

items.question: Someone you know is getting piled on in the comments, and it's getting mean. What do you do?

choices.text: Jump in and fight back for them in the comments.
Don't join in. Check on them privately, and tell an adult if it keeps going.
Scroll past. It's not your fight.
Like a few of the comments so they leave you alone.

hints: Which choice doesn't add fuel?
Which one actually helps the person getting piled on?
items.reasoning: Staying out of the fight and getting help protects them and you. That's Be Safe.

distractors.A: Fighting in the comments usually makes the pile bigger.
distractors.C: It might not be your fight. It's still someone you know.
distractors.D: Joining in to stay safe makes you part of it.

items.question: For a couple of weeks, something has felt off, and it's more than one bad day. What's the best step?

choices.text: Keep it to yourself. Everyone has bad weeks.
Wait. It will probably pass on its own.
Post something vague and see who notices.
Tell an adult you trust.

hints: Which choice gets someone on your side?
Is "a couple of weeks" still just a bad day?
items.reasoning: Saying so early is how things start to get better. That's Be Safe.

distractors.A: Everyone does have bad weeks. That's exactly why there are adults whose job is to help.
distractors.B: Waiting is how a couple of weeks turns into a couple of months.
distractors.C: Hoping someone notices is a hard way to ask. Asking straight works better.

mystery.title: The Case of the Second-Half Comeback
mystery.intro: Friday night. The Hawks are down 21–3 at halftime. They win 24–21. By Saturday morning, three stories are going around. The coach: "It was my halftime speech." A fan: "The wind died down." The quarterback: "We switched to short passes." Which story does the evidence back up? Work the case. (This case is made up. The skills are real.)
mystery.underneath: claim, evidence and explanation. You use the same skills when you explain why something happened in Social Studies.

items.question: Three people explain the comeback. What do all three explanations have in common?

choices.text: They're all right.
Each one is a claim: an explanation that still needs evidence.
The coach's is true, because he's the coach.
The quarterback's is true, because he played.

hints: Has anyone shown proof yet?
What's the difference between saying why and showing why?
items.reasoning: A claim is an explanation you still have to back up. Until there's evidence, all three are just claims. That's claim and evidence.

distractors.A: They can't all be the whole reason. The evidence has to sort them.
distractors.C: Being in charge doesn't make an explanation true.
distractors.D: Being there helps, but it still needs evidence.

items.question: The stat sheet: first half, 4 of 15 long passes caught. Second half, 14 of 17 short passes caught. Which claim does this support?

choices.text: The coach's speech.
The wind dying down.
The switch to short passes.
None of them.

hints: What changed between the halves on the sheet?
Which claim is about passing?
items.reasoning: The sheet shows the switch and what it did. Evidence supports a claim when it matches what the claim says changed.

distractors.A: A stat sheet can't show what was said in the locker room.
distractors.B: The sheet shows what kind of passes, not the weather.
distractors.D: It clearly backs one of them.

items.question: The fan says the wind died down. The weather report shows a steady wind, about 5 miles an hour, all night. What does that do to the fan's claim?

choices.text: Weakens it. The wind didn't change, so it can't explain what changed.
Proves it.
It doesn't matter.
Proves the coach was right.

hints: Did the wind change between the halves?
Can something that stayed the same explain a change?
items.reasoning: Evidence can knock a claim out too. If nothing changed, it can't explain the change.

distractors.B: The report shows the opposite of what the fan said.
distractors.C: It matters. It rules one story out.
distractors.D: The weather report says nothing about the speech.

items.question: The coach's speech could still have helped. Can a comeback have more than one cause?

choices.text: No. There's only ever one reason.
Yes, and all three count the same.
No. Speeches never matter.
Yes. The play change has the strongest evidence, but the speech may have helped too.

hints: Does the stat sheet rule out the speech?
Which cause has the most evidence behind it?
items.reasoning: Big events usually have more than one cause. Rank them by the evidence. That's explanation.

distractors.A: Most comebacks, and most of history, have more than one cause.
distractors.B: Not the same. The wind story was knocked out, and the speech has no evidence yet.
distractors.C: It might have mattered. There's just no evidence either way yet.

items.question: A friend posts: "Coach's speech won the game!!" What's the most helpful reply?

choices.text: Like it. It's a nice story.
"Nope, you're wrong."
"The speech might've helped, but the stat sheet shows the switch to short passes made the difference."
Say nothing.

hints: Which reply uses the evidence?
Which one would you want to get?
items.reasoning: Give the evidence, keep it friendly, and leave room for other causes. That's Be Respectful and Be Responsible at once.

distractors.A: A nice story isn't the same as what happened.
distractors.B: True or not, it gives your friend no reason to change their mind.
distractors.D: Then the story everyone remembers is the one with no evidence.

proof_questions: What was the score at halftime?
In the second half, how many short passes were caught?
What did the weather report say about the wind?
